meta.moduleTitle: 09.4 KINS 4403: Anaerobic and Aerobic Power Training Programs

pages.title: Part 1: The Energy System Continuum and Interval Training Fundamentals
pages.readingHtml:
The Energy System Continuum and Group Exercise Training

Anaerobic and aerobic power training programs operate along a physiological energy system continuum. At one extreme, short sprint events (e.g., \(100\text{ m}\) dash) rely almost exclusively on high-power ATP resynthesis via the ATP-phosphocreatine (ATP-PCr) system. As event duration increases through middle-distance running, primary metabolic reliance shifts to the anaerobic glycolytic system. At the far end of the continuum, long-distance events (e.g., \(42.2\text{ km}\) marathon) depend predominantly on the oxidative phosphorylation system. However, even at extreme event durations, multiple energy systems interact to support total ATP turnover.

First popularized by Dr. Kenneth Cooper in \(1968\), group exercise training initially focused on rhythmic dance movements choreographed to music to promote disease prevention. Modern group exercise formats span cardiovascular, strength, and flexibility disciplines, incorporating high-intensity interval classes, indoor cycling, aquatic workouts, and functional resistance training. Participation in structured group fitness yields substantial cardiovascular and metabolic adaptations, including increased maximal oxygen consumption (\(\dot{V}\text{O}_{2\max}\)), elevated high-density lipoprotein (\(HDL\)) cholesterol, increased lean muscle mass, and reduced fasting blood glucose, low-density lipoprotein (\(LDL\)) cholesterol, blood triglycerides, and body fat mass.

Fundamentals and Variables of Interval Training

Interval training consists of repeated bouts of high- to moderate-intensity exercise interspersed with structured rest or active recovery intervals. By inserting recovery periods between intense exercise bouts, athletes can perform a significantly greater total volume of high-intensity work compared to continuous exertion.

Designing an interval training prescription requires manipulating six core physiological variables:

  • Rate (Intensity) of the Exercise Interval: Established via target completion times for set distances or as a percentage of maximal heart rate (\(\text{HR}_{\max}\)). ATP-PCr development requires near-maximal intensity (\(90\%\text{ to }98\%\) velocity or \(90\%\text{ to }100\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\)); glycolytic development requires high intensity (\(80\%\text{ to }95\%\) velocity or \(85\%\text{ to }100\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\)); oxidative development requires moderate-to-high intensity (\(75\%\text{ to }85\%\) velocity or \(70\%\text{ to }90\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\)).
  • Distance or Duration of the Exercise Interval: Dictated by event specificity, ranging from short \(30\text{ to }200\text{ m}\) sprints for speed athletes up to \(400\text{ to }1,500\text{ m}\) bouts for distance runners.
  • Number of Repetitions and Sets: Shorter, higher-intensity intervals necessitate a greater number of repetitions and sets, whereas longer distance intervals feature reduced repetition counts.
  • Duration of Rest or Active Recovery Interval: Determined by heart rate recovery. For athletes \(\le 30\text{ years of age}\), heart rate should drop to between \(130\text{ and }150\text{ beats/min}\) before initiating the next work interval. For athletes \(> 30\text{ years}\), the target range is adjusted by subtracting \(\text{Age} - 30\) from both boundaries. Inter-set recovery should allow heart rate to fall below \(120\text{ beats/min}\).
  • Type of Activity During Recovery: Ranging from passive rest to walking, slow jogging, or easy swimming. Higher exercise interval intensities require lower active recovery intensities.
  • Training Frequency: Ranging from \(2\text{ to }4\text{ days/week}\) for team-sport conditioning up to \(5\text{ to }7\text{ days/week}\) for elite sprinters and swimmers.

Clinical / Coaching Application

When prescribing interval training for an athlete over \(30\text{ years of age}\), coaches must adjust target recovery heart rate thresholds to account for age-related declines in maximal heart rate (\(\sim 1\text{ beat/min per year}\)). For a \(45\text{-year-old}\) athlete, subtract \(15\text{ beats/min}\) (\(45 - 30\)) from standard recovery boundaries, yielding a work-interval re-entry heart rate of \(115\text{ to }135\text{ beats/min}\).

pages.title: Part 2: Continuous Training, LSD, Fartlek, and Interval-Circuit Training
pages.readingHtml:
Continuous Training Modalities: LSD, High-Intensity, and Fartlek

Continuous training involves sustained physical activity without intervening rest periods, targeting adaptations primarily within the oxidative and glycolytic energy systems. Continuous training formats span a broad spectrum of intensities and physiological objectives:

  • High-Intensity Continuous Training: Performed at work rates representing \(85\%\text{ to }95\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\), operating at, near, or slightly above the athlete's lactate threshold. Because elite endurance athletes (such as marathon runners) race at or near their lactate threshold, high-intensity continuous bouts provide critical pace-specific metabolic conditioning.
  • Long, Slow Distance (LSD) Training: Pioneered in the 1920s by Dr. Ernst van Aaken, LSD training features continuous exercise at relatively low intensities (\(60\%\text{ to }80\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\), corresponding to \(50\%\text{ to }75\%\text{ }\dot{V}\text{O}_{2\max}\)). Distance and volume are prioritized over speed, with marathon runners accumulating \(15\text{ to }30\text{ miles/day}\) (\(24\text{ to }48\text{ km/day}\)) and \(100\text{ to }200\text{ miles/week}\). While LSD is the safest aerobic conditioning mode for sedentary individuals and team-sport off-season maintenance, excessive LSD training increases overuse injury risk and fails to develop maximal leg speed.
  • Fartlek Training: Developed in Sweden in the 1930s (meaning "speed play"), Fartlek training is an unscripted continuous modality where the athlete alternates speeds spontaneously over varied natural terrain (hills, trails). Fartlek provides psychological variety while engaging both aerobic and anaerobic pathways.

Interval-Circuit Training

Interval-circuit training combines the metabolic demands of interval running with the muscular endurance and strength benefits of circuit training. Developed in Scandinavia during the 1960s and 1970s, an interval-circuit course spans \(3,000\text{ to }10,000\text{ m}\), featuring exercise stations placed every \(400\text{ to }1,600\text{ m}\). Athletes jog, run, or sprint between stations, stopping at each station to perform targeted strength, flexibility, or muscular endurance exercises before resuming running.

Continuous / Combination ModalityIntensity Domain (% HRmax)Primary Energy System AdaptationKey Physiological Benefits & Risks
High-Intensity Continuous\(85\%\text{--}95\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\)Oxidative & Anaerobic GlycolyticEnhances lactate threshold velocity; pace-specific race preparation.
Long, Slow Distance (LSD)\(60\%\text{--}80\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\)Oxidative PhosphorylationIncreases mitochondrial density & fat oxidation; high overuse injury risk.
Fartlek TrainingUnscripted (\(60\%\text{--}95\%\text{ HR}_{\max}\))Mixed Oxidative, Glycolytic, & ATP-PCrImproves terrain adaptability and mental engagement; flexible structure.
Interval-Circuit TrainingVaried sprint & station workOxidative, Glycolytic, & Local MuscularDevelops concurrent aerobic capacity, muscular endurance, and functional strength.
Clinical / Coaching Application

While long, slow distance (LSD) training is effective for health-related cardiovascular conditioning and base building, endurance athletes cannot rely on LSD exclusively. To elevate race-pace running economy and muscle power, coaches must integrate high-intensity continuous runs at or near the lactate threshold alongside structured interval sessions.

pages.title: Part 3: High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Health and Athletics
pages.readingHtml:
High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) Kinetics and Health Adaptations

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) consists of brief, repeated bursts of maximal or near-maximal exercise interspersed with periods of rest or low-intensity recovery. Research led by scientists at McMaster University demonstrated that Wingate-based sprint interval protocols—consisting of \(4\text{ to }6\) bouts of \(30\text{ s}\) all-out cycling interspersed with \(4.5\text{ min}\) of recovery—produce physiological adaptations comparable to traditional continuous endurance training despite a fraction of the total time commitment.

Remarkably, performing just \(6\text{ HIIT sessions}\) over a \(2\text{-week span}\) (accumulating only \(15\text{ min}\) of total all-out exercise within a \(2.5\text{ h}\) total time commitment) significantly increases maximal oxygen uptake (\(\dot{V}\text{O}_{2\max}\)), skeletal muscle oxidative enzyme activity (e.g., citrate synthase, pyruvate dehydrogenase), mitochondrial biogenesis, and peripheral muscle membrane transport proteins (such as \(GLUT\text{-}4\) and monocarboxylate transporters). In clinical populations, HIIT enhances insulin sensitivity, glycemic control, and vascular endothelial function in individuals with or at risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

HIIT for Endurance Athletes and Team Sports

In highly trained endurance athletes who have reached a plateau under high-volume aerobic training, increasing training intensity close to or above \(\dot{V}\text{O}_{2\max}\) is required to drive further performance gains. Replacing \(15\%\text{ of normal training time}\) with HIIT over \(4\text{ weeks}\) significantly increases peak power output and \(4\text{ km}\) time-trial speed in competitive cyclists. Furthermore, employing the 10-20-30 concept (\(5\text{ min}\) blocks alternating \(30\text{ s}\) low speed, \(20\text{ s}\) moderate speed, and \(10\text{ s}\) maximal sprint) for \(7\text{ weeks}\) increases \(\dot{V}\text{O}_{2\max}\) by \(4\%\) and improves \(1,500\text{ m}\) and \(5\text{ km}\) running performance despite a \(\sim 50\%\) reduction in total weekly training volume.

For endurance athletes, evidence-based recommendations suggest structuring annual training volume such that \(75\%\) of total volume is performed at continuous low intensities, while \(10\%\text{ to }15\%\) is devoted to high-intensity interval workouts. In elite team-sport athletes (e.g., professional soccer players), a \(5\text{-week}\) HIIT protocol consisting of \(6\text{ to }9\) bouts of \(30\text{ s}\) intervals at \(90\%\text{ to }95\%\text{ }\dot{V}\text{O}_{2\max}\) produces substantial improvements in high-intensity shuttle-run capacity (\(+11\%\)) and running economy (reduced submaximal oxygen cost at \(10\text{ km/h}\)) without inducing overtraining.

Clinical / Coaching Application

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) offers a potent stimulus for improving running economy, peak power, and cardiovascular health in both clinical patients and elite athletes. Coaches should adhere to the \(75\text{--}15\text{ rule}\) for endurance periodization—maintaining \(75\%\) of training volume at low continuous aerobic intensities and allocating \(10\%\text{ to }15\%\) to high-intensity intervals—to maximize performance gains while minimizing the risk of overtraining syndrome.

glossary.def: Instruction-led aerobic, strength, or flexibility exercise sessions performed in a group setting, originally conceptualized by Dr. Kenneth Cooper for disease prevention.
A training system consisting of repeated bouts of high- to moderate-intensity exercise interspersed with periods of rest or reduced-intensity active recovery.
Uninterrupted exercise performed without rest intervals, ranging from long slow distance (LSD) to high-intensity continuous workouts at race pace.
Continuous low-intensity aerobic training (60% to 80% HRmax, 50% to 75% VO2max) prioritizing high workout distance and duration over speed.
Continuous exercise ('speed play') developed in Sweden in which the athlete continuously alters pace from high speed to jogging across varied natural terrain.
A combined training modality featuring interval running between stations where strength, flexibility, or muscular endurance exercises are performed.
Exercise training consisting of brief, repeated bursts of maximal or near-maximal effort interspersed with short periods of rest or low-intensity recovery.
A specific HIIT framework consisting of 5-minute continuous blocks alternating 30 seconds of low speed, 20 seconds of moderate speed, and 10 seconds of maximal speed.
The oxygen cost of running at a given submaximal velocity, representing metabolic efficiency during locomotion.
